The wheel, and the speed taken from it:\n```python\nloader.load_wheel()\n```\n\n```python\nspeed = trial_traces(wheel.times, np.abs(wheel.velocity), stim_on)\n```\n\niii. The reference derives `'wheel-speed'` the same way, as `np.abs` of the velocity that `SessionLoader` returns.\n\n## 7-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *wheel_speed*?\n\ni. Three steps. The wheel is recorded only when it moves, so `SessionLoader` first interpolates the position onto an even 1000 Hz grid and differentiates it into a velocity, applying a 20 Hz Butterworth low pass while doing so; the speed is the absolute value of that velocity, in radians per second. That trace is then resampled onto the 100 bin centres of each trial. Finally it is cut into three classes at the 33rd and 67th percentile of the session, so the three classes are equally sized within a session.\n\nii. What `SessionLoader.load_wheel` does internally:\n```python\nself.wheel['position'], self.wheel['times'] = interpolate_position(\n    wheel_raw['timestamps'], wheel_raw['position'], freq=fs)\nself.wheel['velocity'], self.wheel['acceleration'] = velocity_filtered(\n    self.wheel['position'], fs=fs, corner_frequency=corner_frequency, order=order)\n```\n\nResampling onto the bin centres, then splitting into three:\n```python\ntraces.append(np.interp(onset + TIME, times[first:last], values[first:last]))\n```\n\n```python\nSPLIT = [100 / 3, 2 * 100 / 3]       # equal sized classes, from percentiles of each session's own trace\n\ndef discretize(trace):\n    \"\"\"Equal sized classes, split at percentiles of this session's own trace.\"\"\"\n    return np.digitize(trace, np.percentile(trace, SPLIT))\n```\n\niii. The interpolation and the filter are not choices, they are what the IBL documentation recommends for computing wheel velocity and what `SessionLoader` does by default, so the reference and this conversion get the same trace.\n\n## 7-d. How is `output` *wheel_speed* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. The wheel trace is sampled at the same 100 bin centres as the neural data, measured from the same stimulus onset, so the two share a time axis bin for bin.\n\nii. The bin centres, and the wheel evaluated at them:\n```python\nTIME = EDGES[:-1] + BIN / 2                              # bin centres, the first decoder input\n```\n\n```python\ntraces.append(np.interp(onset + TIME, times[first:last], values[first:last]))\n```\n\niii. The wheel is on the same session clock as the spikes, so evaluating it at the bin centres is all the alignment needed.\n\n## 8-a. What variables in the raw data is `output` *whisker_motion_energy* derived from?\n\ni. The motion energy of a side camera, `<side>Camera.ROIMotionEnergy` with its frame times `_ibl_<side>Camera.times`. It is a single value per video frame, computed by IBL over a square covering the whisker pad, and is used as released. The left camera is taken when the session has it and the right otherwise.\n\nii. Choosing the camera, and loading it:\n```python\ndef camera_view(eid):\n    \"\"\"The side camera this session has whisker motion energy for, left preferred.\"\"\"\n    for view in ('left', 'right'):\n        if len(one.list_datasets(eid, filename=f'{view}Camera.ROIMotionEnergy.npy',\n                                 query_type='local')):\n            return view\n```\n\n```python\nloader.load_motion_energy(views=[view])\n```\n\niii. This follows the logic of the reference paer.\n\n## 8-b. What processing is involved in computing `output` *whisker_motion_energy*?\n\ni. The released trace is used as it is, with no filtering or normalisation. It is resampled onto the 100 bin centres of each trial and then cut into three classes at the 33rd and 67th percentile of the session, the same rule as the wheel.\n\nii. Resampling onto the bin centres, then splitting into three:\n```python\nwhisker = trial_traces(motion_energy.times, motion_energy.iloc[:, 1], stim_on)\n```\n\n```python\ndef discretize(trace):\n    \"\"\"Equal sized classes, split at percentiles of this session's own trace.\"\"\"\n    return np.digitize(trace, np.percentile(trace, SPLIT))\n```\n\niii. No additional processing.\n\n## 8-d. How is `output` *whisker_motion_energy* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. The camera trace is sampled at the same 100 bin centres as the neural data, measured from the same stimulus onset, so the two share a time axis bin for bin.\n\nii. The camera evaluated at the bin centres:\n```python\ntraces.append(np.interp(onset + TIME, times[first:last], values[first:last]))\n```\n\niii. The camera frame times are on the same session clock as the neural data, so evaluating the trace at the bin centres is all the alignment needed.\n\n## 9. How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?\n\ni. The API handles most of it. Missing data is dropped: A trial whose window is not spanned by the wheel or the camera is dropped; A session left with no unit or fewer than two trials is dropped.\n\nii. Skipping an unreleased probe:\n```python\n# a session can hold an insertion whose spike sorting was never released\nif not clusters:\n    continue\n```\n\nDropping a session with nothing usable data:\n```python\nif res['n_units'] == 0 or res['n_trials'] < 2:\n    print('skipped %s: %d trials, %d units'\n          % (res['session_id'][:8], res['n_trials'], res['n_units']), flush=True)\n    continue\n```\n\nThe coverage test for wheel and camera data:\n```python\ninside = begin <= end\nfirst = np.where(inside, times[np.clip(begin, 0, times.size - 1)], np.inf)\nlast = np.where(inside, times[np.clip(end, 0, times.size - 1)], -np.inf)\nreturn inside & (np.abs(start - first) <= BIN) & (np.abs(stop - last) <= BIN)\n```\n\niii. Mostly are missing data that we drop from the final results.\n\n## 10-a. What are the most time-consuming steps of the code?\n\ni. Reading the spike sorting off disk, dominated by the two spike arrays of a probe that between them run to hundreds of megabytes.\n\nii. Reading the spike sorting, the one expensive call:\n```python\nspikes, clusters, channels = loader.load_spike_sorting(check_hash=False)\n```\n\niii. The cost is mainly file I/O.\n\n## 10-b. What loops in the code could have been vectorized to improve efficiency?\n\ni. Two loops run once per trial, one resampling the behavioural traces and one binning the spikes. Both could be written as a single call over all trials at once, the binning by offsetting each spike's index by its trial and the resampling by building one query vector. Neither was, because each trial is a slice of a different part of the session and the loop keeps that obvious; they cost about 0.1 s a session between them, so there is nothing to gain.\n\nii. The two per trial loops:\n```python\nfor trial, onset in enumerate(stim_on):\n    spike_time = times[begin[trial]:end[trial]] - onset      # time from stimulus onset\n```\n\n```python\nfor trial, onset in enumerate(stim_on):\n    first = max(begin[trial] - 1, 0)\n```\n\niii. Not really. Nothing that can improve the code significantly.\n\n## 10-c. What processing does the code repeat multiple times?\n\ni. N/A\n\nii. N/A\n\niii. N/A\n\n## 10-d. What unnecessary processing does the code do that is discarded in downstream analyses?\n\ni. N/A\n\nii. N/A\n\niii. N/A\n\n## 10-e. How is memory usage optimized?\n\ni. The neural array is cast to float32 and the outputs to int8, which is where nearly all the size is. Sessions are held one at a time in each worker rather than all at once, and only the two spike arrays the conversion needs are read, which keeps the peak of a worker at about 3 GB on a two probe session.\n\nii. The casts, where the arrays are built:\n```python\nneural = [trial.astype(np.float32) for trial in rate]\n```\n\n```python\noutputs.append(np.stack([np.full(N_BINS, row.choice), np.full(N_BINS, row.prior),\n                         speed_class[trial], whisker_class[trial]]).astype(np.int8))\n```\n\niii. Sessions are held one at a time in each worker rather than all at once.\n\"\"\"Convert the IBL brain-wide map into the decoder format.\n\nUsage: python -u convert_data.py <outpicklefile> [--full | --sample] [--datadir DIR]\n\"\"\"\n\nimport argparse\nimport datetime\nimport os\nimport pickle\nimport time\nimport warnings\nfrom concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor, as_completed\n\nimport numpy as np\nimport pandas as pd\nfrom tqdm import tqdm\n\n_zhang2025_seed = 'x5cidj2hy87s'\nnp.random.seed(sum(ord(c) for c in _zhang2025_seed) % 2**31)\n\n# the loader always pulls these four spike arrays\nimport brainbox.io.one as bio\nbio.SPIKES_ATTRIBUTES = ['clusters', 'times']\n\nfrom one.api import ONE, One\nfrom one.alf.exceptions import ALFWarning\nfrom brainbox.io.one import SessionLoader, SpikeSortingLoader\nfrom iblatlas.regions import BrainRegions\n\n# the trials table and the spike sorting are each listed at two revisions, and ONE warns\n# once per load that it is taking the later one, which is the one we want\nwarnings.filterwarnings('ignore', category=ALFWarning)\n\n# --- constants ---\n\nHERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))\n# Directory holding the one_cache/ folder.  'trial_in_block': trials.groupby(block).cumcount()})\n\n\ndef covered(times, stim_on):\n    \"\"\"Trials whose window is spanned by this stream, allowing the one bin gap the reference allows.\"\"\"\n - 1       # last sample inside the window\n\n    # a trial with no sample at all, or a gap at either edge, has no usable trace\n    inside = begin <= end\n    first = np.where(inside, trials.stimOn_times.to_numpy()\n    reaction = trials.firstMovement_times.to_numpy() - stim_on\n\n    keep = (reaction >= MIN_RT) & (reaction <= MAX_RT)          # NaN compares false, so those go too\n    keep &= trials.choice.isin(CHOICE).to_numpy()               # drops the no response trials\n    keep &= trials.probabilityLeft.isin(PRIOR).to_numpy()\n\n    return keep & covered(wheel_times, stim_on) & covered(camera_times, stim_on)\n\n\n# --- behavior ---\n\ndef window_slice(times, stim_on):\n    \"\"\"Index range of each trial window, so a stream is sliced rather than rescanned per trial.\"\"\"\n    window_start = stim_on + T_START\n    window_stop = stim_on + T_STOP\n\n    # the samples are in time order, so each window is one contiguous range of them\n    begin = np.abs(wheel.velocity), stim_on)\n    whisker = trial_traces(motion_energy.times, motion_energy.iloc[:, 1], stim_on)\n\n    spike_times, spike_units, regions = load_neural(eid)\n    rate = spike_counts(spike_times, spike_units, regions.size, stim_on) / BIN\n\n#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"\nConvert the IBL brain-wide map (BWM) public dataset into the decoder-compatible\ndictionary format described in the task specification.\n\nUsage\n-----\n    python -u /app/convert_data.py <outpicklefile> [--full | --sample]\n                                   [--show-processing] [--n-workers N]\n\nOptions\n-------\n    --full             process every session of the BWM freeze (default)\n    --sample           process only 2 sessions (quick end-to-end test)\n    --show-processing  save a bin, with the reference's\n    interval-coverage checks\n\nDeviations from the reference caching script, and why, are documented in\n/app/CONVERSION_NOTES.md (Step 4/5). The main ones:\n  * neurons are restricted to IBL well-isolated units (`label >= 1`) in grey\n    matter (Beryl acronym not in {root, void}), following the data paper\n  * trials whose behaviour window contains NaN are dropped instead of being\n    NaN-imputed at model-fit time\n  * the continuous behaviours are discretised into per-session tertiles, as\n    required by the categorical-output specification\n\"\"\"\n\nimport argparse\nimport os\nimport pickle\nimport sys\nimport time\nimport traceback\nimport warnings\nfrom collections import defaultdict\n\nimport numpy as np\nimport pandas as pd\n\n# reference code from the method paper\nsys.path.insert(0, '/app/code/code_zhang2025/src')\n\nfrom scipy.interpolate import interp1d\n\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\n# constants -- these mirror `params` in code_zhang2025/src/0_data_caching.py\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\nPARAMS = {\n    'interval_len': 2.0,\n    'binsize': 0.02,\n    'single_region': False,\n    'align_time': 'stimOn_times',\n    'time_window': (-0.5, 1.5),\n}\nN_BINS = int(np.ceil(PARAMS['interval_len'] / PARAMS['binsize']))  # 100\n\nBWM_FREEZE = '/app/code/code_zhang2025/data/bwm_release.csv'\nONE_TABLES_DIR = '/app/data/one_cache/Brainwidemap'\nONE_BASE_URL = 'https://openalyx.internationalbrainlab.org'\n\n#: Beryl acronyms that are not grey-matter brain regions.\nNON_REGION_ACRONYMS = ('root', 'void')\n\n#: quantiles used to discretise the continuous behaviours into 3 classes\nTERTILES = (1.0 / 3.0, 2.0 / 3.0)\n\n#: minimum number of retained neurons for a session to be kept. The data paper\n#: restricts analyses to \"regions that ... contained at least five well-isolated\n#: neurons per session\"; here the decoded population is the whole session, so the\n#: same floor is applied at the session level.\nMIN_NEURONS_PER_SESSION = 5\n\nOUTPUT_NAMES = ['choice', 'prior', 'wheel_speed', 'whisker_motion_energy']\nOUTPUT_VALUES = [\n    ['left', 'right'],\n    ['0.2 (right block)', '0.5 (unbiased)', '0.8 (left block)'],\n    ['low', 'medium', 'high'],\n    ['low', 'medium', 'high'],\n]\nINPUT_NAMES = ['time_from_stim_onset_s', 'trial_number_in_block']\n\n\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\n# per-worker singletons\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\n_ONE = None\n_BRAIN_REGIONS = None\n\n\ndef get_one():\n    \"\"\"Return this process's ONE client (created once, offline-friendly).\"\"\"\n    global _ONE\n    if _ONE is None:\n        from one.api import ONE\n        _ONE = ONE(base_url=ONE_BASE_URL, silent=True, tables_dir=ONE_TABLES_DIR)\n    return _ONE\n\n\ndef get_brain_regions():\n    global _BRAIN_REGIONS\n    if _BRAIN_REGIONS is None:\n        from iblatlas.regions import BrainRegions\n        _BRAIN_REGIONS = BrainRegions()\n    return _BRAIN_REGIONS\n\n\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\n# loading\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\ndef load_session_spikes(one, eid, probe_rows):\n    \"\"\"Load and merge the spike sorting of every probe of a session.\n\n    Mirrors ``ibl_data_utils.prepare_data`` (minus the raw-ephys sampling-rate\n    query, which requires streaming the raw binary from the remote server).\n\n    Returns\n    -------\n    spikes : dict with 'times', 'clusters', ... (spike-time sorted, merged)\n    clusters : pandas.DataFrame, one row per cluster, re-indexed across probes\n    \"\"\"\n    from brainbox.io.one import SpikeSortingLoader\n    from utils.ibl_data_utils import merge_probes\n\n    spikes_list, clusters_list = [], []\n    for _, row in probe_rows.iterrows():\n        ssl = SpikeSortingLoader(pid=row.pid, one=one, eid=eid, pname=row.probe_name)\n        sp, cl, ch = ssl.load_spike_sorting()\n        cl_df = SpikeSortingLoader.merge_clusters(sp, cl, ch, compute_metrics=False).to_df()\n        cl_df['pid'] = row.pid\n        spikes_list.append(sp)\n        clusters_list.append(cl_df)\n    return merge_probes(spikes_list, clusters_list)\n\n\ndef select_neurons(clusters):\n    \"\"\"Well-isolated units (IBL ``label >= 1``) located in grey matter.\n\n    ``label`` is the fraction of the three RIGOR single-unit metrics passed\n    (amplitude > 50 uV, noise cut-off < 20 uV, refractory-period violation), so\n    ``label >= 1`` is exactly the data paper's \"well-isolated neuron\".\n\n    Returns\n    -------\n    keep_idx : (n_kept,) int array of row indices into `clusters`\n    beryl : (n_kept,) array of Beryl acronyms for the kept clusters\n    n_good : number of well-isolated units before the grey-matter restriction\n    \"\"\"\n    br = get_brain_regions()\n    beryl_all = np.asarray(br.acronym2acronym(clusters['acronym'].to_numpy(), mapping='Beryl'))\n    good = clusters['label'].to_numpy() >= 1\n    in_brain = ~np.isin(beryl_all, NON_REGION_ACRONYMS)\n    keep = good & in_brain\n    keep_idx = np.nonzero(keep)[0]\n    return keep_idx, beryl_all[keep_idx], int(good.sum())\n\n\ndef load_trials(one, eid):\n    \"\"\"Trials table + reference trial mask (``load_trials_and_mask``).\"\"\"\n    from brainbox.io.one import SessionLoader\n    from utils.ibl_data_utils import load_trials_and_mask\n\n    sess_loader = SessionLoader(one=one, eid=eid)\n    trials, mask = load_trials_and_mask(one=one, eid=eid, max_trial_len=10.0,\n                                        sess_loader=sess_loader)\n    return sess_loader, trials, mask.to_numpy()\n\n\ndef load_continuous_behaviors(one, eid, sess_loader):\n    \"\"\"Wheel speed and whisker motion energy for the whole session.\n\n    Same sources as ``ibl_data_utils.load_target_behavior``:\n    wheel speed = |velocity| from ``SessionLoader.load_wheel`` (1 kHz,\n    Gaussian-smoothed), whisker motion energy from the left camera ROI motion\n    energy, falling back to the right camera when the left is unavailable.\n    \"\"\"\n    beh = {}\n\n    sess_loader.load_wheel()\n    beh['wheel-speed'] = {\n        'times': sess_loader.wheel['times'].to_numpy(),\n        'values': np.abs(sess_loader.wheel['velocity'].to_numpy()),\n        'source': 'wheel.velocity (abs)',\n    }\n\n    me = None\n    for view, cam in (('left', 'leftCamera'), ('right', 'rightCamera')):\n        try:\n            sess_loader.load_motion_energy(views=[view])\n            df = sess_loader.motion_energy[cam]\n            me = {\n                'times': df['times'].to_numpy(),\n                'values': df['whiskerMotionEnergy'].to_numpy(),\n                'source': f'{cam}.ROIMotionEnergy',\n            }\n            break\n        except Exception:\n            continue\n    if me is None:\n        raise RuntimeError('no whisker motion energy available (left or right camera)')\n    beh['whisker-motion-energy'] = me\n    return beh\n\n\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\n# binning / interpolation\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\ndef bin_spikes(spike_times, spike_clusters, n_neurons, interval_begs, binsize=0.02,\n               n_bins=N_BINS):\n    \"\"\"Spike counts in non-overlapping bins for every interval.\n\n    Reproduces ``bincount2D(times, clusters, xbin=binsize, xlim=[t_beg, t_end])``\n    truncated to the first ``n_bins`` columns: bin ``k`` of a trial covers\n    ``[t_beg + k*binsize, t_beg + (k+1)*binsize)`` and only spikes with\n    ``t_beg <= t < t_end`` are counted.\n\n    `spike_times` must be sorted and `spike_clusters` must already be remapped\n    to 0..n_neurons-1.\n\n    Returns (n_intervals, n_neurons, n_bins) float32 array of counts.\n    \"\"\"\n    n_intervals = len(interval_begs)\n    out = np.zeros((n_intervals, n_neurons, n_bins), dtype=np.float32)\n    interval_ends = interval_begs + n_bins * binsize\n    i0s = np.searchsorted(spike_times, interval_begs, side='left')\n    i1s = np.searchsorted(spike_times, interval_ends, side='left')\n    for k in range(n_intervals):\n        i0, i1 = i0s[k], i1s[k]\n        if i1 <= i0:\n            continue\n        rel = spike_times[i0:i1] - interval_begs[k]\n        bin_idx = np.floor(rel / binsize).astype(np.int64)\n        np.clip(bin_idx, 0, n_bins - 1, out=bin_idx)\n        flat = spike_clusters[i0:i1].astype(np.int64) * n_bins + bin_idx\n        counts = np.bincount(flat, minlength=n_neurons * n_bins)\n        out[k] = counts.reshape(n_neurons, n_bins)\n    return out\n\n\ndef interpolate_behavior(times, values, interval_begs, binsize=0.02, n_bins=N_BINS):\n    \"\"\"Interpolate a continuous behaviour onto each trial's bin grid.\n\n    Follows ``ibl_data_utils.get_behavior_per_interval``: samples strictly\n    inside the interval are selected, then linearly interpolated (with\n    extrapolation) onto ``linspace(t_beg + binsize, t_end, n_bins)``, i.e. the\n    right edge of each spike bin.\n\n    Returns\n    -------\n    vals : (n_intervals, n_bins) float array (rows of NaN where invalid)\n    good : (n_intervals,) bool array\n    reasons : list of str or None, per interval\n    \"\"\"\n    interval_ends = interval_begs + n_bins * binsize\n    idxs_beg = np.searchsorted(times, interval_begs, side='right')\n    idxs_end = np.searchsorted(times, interval_ends, side='left')\n\n    n = len(interval_begs)\n    vals = np.full((n, n_bins), np.nan, dtype=np.float64)\n    good = np.zeros(n, dtype=bool)\n    reasons = [None] * n\n\n    for k in range(n):\n        t = times[idxs_beg[k]:idxs_end[k]]\n        v = values[idxs_beg[k]:idxs_end[k]]\n        if len(v) == 0:\n            reasons[k] = 'target data not present'\n            continue\n        if np.isnan(interval_begs[k]) or np.isnan(interval_ends[k]):\n            reasons[k] = 'bad interval data'\n            continue\n        if np.abs(interval_begs[k] - t[0]) > binsize:\n            reasons[k] = 'target data starts too late'\n            continue\n        if np.abs(interval_ends[k] - t[-1]) > binsize:\n            reasons[k] = 'target data ends too early'\n            continue\n        if np.any(np.isnan(v)):\n            # the reference keeps these (allow_nans=True) and imputes the trial\n            # mean inside its data loader; a categorical target cannot be\n            # imputed without inventing a class, so the trial is dropped\n            reasons[k] = 'nans in target data'\n            continue\n        x = np.linspace(interval_begs[k] + binsize, interval_ends[k], n_bins)\n        vals[k] = interp1d(t, v, kind='linear', fill_value='extrapolate')(x)\n        good[k] = True\n    return vals, good, reasons\n\n\ndef discretize_tertiles(values):\n    \"\"\"Map a (n_trials, n_bins) continuous array onto {0, 1, 2} by tertile.\n\n    Thresholds are the 33.3 / 66.7 percentiles of all values pooled over the\n    session's retained trials, so each session's classes are balanced and the\n    arbitrary units of motion energy do not have to be comparable across\n    sessions.\n    \"\"\"\n    flat = values.reshape(-1)\n    q1, q2 = np.quantile(flat, TERTILES)\n    if not (q1 < q2):\n        # degenerate (heavily tied) distribution: fall back to the distinct\n        # quantile values that do exist so the labels stay monotone\n        edges = np.unique([q1, q2])\n        labels = np.digitize(values, edges, right=False)\n        return labels.astype(np.int64), (float(q1), float(q2))\n    labels = np.digitize(values, [q1, q2], right=False).astype(np.int64)\n    return labels, (float(q1), float(q2))\n\n\ndef trial_number_in_block(probability_left):\n    \"\"\"0-based index of each trial within its constant-``probabilityLeft`` block.\n\n    Computed on the *unfiltered* trials table, because the block structure is a\n    property of the experiment, not of which trials survive curation.\n    \"\"\"\n    p = np.asarray(probability_left, dtype=float)\n    # a change (including to/from NaN) starts a new block\n    changed = np.ones(len(p), dtype=bool)\n    if len(p) > 1:\n        same = (p[1:] == p[:-1]) | (np.isnan(p[1:]) & np.isnan(p[:-1]))\n        changed[1:] = ~same\n    block_id = np.cumsum(changed) - 1\n    # index within block = position - position of first trial of that block\n    first_of_block = np.zeros(block_id[-1] + 1, dtype=np.int64)\n    starts = np.nonzero(changed)[0]\n    first_of_block[:] = starts\n    return np.arange(len(p)) - first_of_block[block_id]\n\n\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\n# per-session conversion\n# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------\ndef process_session(task):\n    \"\"\"Convert one session. Returns a dict (or a dict with 'error').\"\"\"\n    eid, probe_rows, subject, lab, show_processing = task\n    t_start = time.time()\n    timings = {}\n    try:\n        warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')\n        one = get_one()\n\n        # ---- neural -------------------------------------------------------\n        t0 = time.time()\n        spikes, clusters = load_session_spikes(one, eid, probe_rows)\n        timings['load_spikes'] = time.time() - t0\n\n        keep_idx, beryl, n_good = select_neurons(clusters)\n        n_neurons = len(keep_idx)\n# Dataset Conversion Notes\n\n## Overview\n- **Dataset**: IBL Brain-Wide Map (BWM) public release — \"A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour\" (IBL et al.), ONE cache staged at `/app/data/one_cache`\n- **Method reference**: Zhang et al. 2026, *Neuron*, \"Exploiting correlations across trials and behavioral sessions to improve neural decoding\" (code in `/app/code/code_zhang2025`)\n- **Date started**: 2026-09-20\n- **Goal**: Convert to decoder-compatible format (`/app/converted_data.pkl`)\n\n---\n\n## Step 0: Setup and Initialization\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\nDirectory contents of `/app`:\n- `CONVERSION_NOTES.md` (this file)\n- `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yaml`, `stage_cache.sh`, `.manifest` — container plumbing\n- `datapaper.pdf` — IBL brain-wide map paper\n- `methodpaper.pdf` — Zhang et al. decoding paper\n- `dataarchitecture.pdf` — IBL data architecture white paper\n- `methods.txt` — excerpts of both papers\n- `code/` — `code_zhang2025/` (method reference code) and `ibllib/` (IBL library source)\n- `data/one_cache/` — ONE cache (release tables + symlinked lab/subject/session ALF trees)\n- `ibl_docs/` — downloaded ONE/ibllib/iblatlas documentation\n- `decoder.py`, `train_decoder.py` — decoder reference implementation and driver\n\nEnvironment verified:\n- `python3` works; ``t_beg <= t < t_end`` are counted.\n   228\t\n   229\t    `spike_times` must be sorted and `spike_clusters` must already be remapped\n   230\t    to 0..n_neurons-1.\n   231\t\n   232\t    Returns (n_intervals, n_neurons, n_bins) float32 array of counts.\n   233\t    \"\"\"\n   234\t    n_intervals = len(interval_begs)\n   235\t    out = np.zeros((n_intervals, n_neurons, n_bins), dtype=np.float32)\n   236\t    interval_ends = interval_begs + n_bins * binsize\n   237\t    i0s = np.searchsorted(spike_times, interval_begs, side='left')\n   238\t    i1s = np.searchsorted(spike_times, interval_ends, side='left')\n   239\t    for k in range(n_intervals):\n   240\t        i0, i1 = i0s[k], i1s[k]\n   241\t        if i1 <= i0:\n   242\t            continue\n   243\t        rel = spike_times[i0:i1] - interval_begs[k]\n   244\t        bin_idx = np.floor(rel / binsize).astype(np.int64)\n   245\t        np.clip(bin_idx, 0, n_bins - 1, out=bin_idx)\n   246\t        flat = spike_clusters[i0:i1].astype(np.int64) * n_bins + bin_idx\n   247\t        counts = np.bincount(flat, minlength=n_neurons * n_bins)\n   248\t        out[k] = counts.reshape(n_neurons, n_bins)\n   249\t    return out\n   250\t\n   251\t\n   252\tdef interpolate_behavior(times, values, interval_begs, binsize=0.02, n_bins=N_BINS):\n   253\t    \"\"\"Interpolate a continuous behaviour onto each trial's bin grid.\n   254\t\n   255\t    Follows ``ibl_data_utils.get_behavior_per_interval``: samples strictly\n   256\t    inside the interval are selected, then linearly interpolated (with\n   257\t    extrapolation) onto ``linspace(t_beg + binsize, t_end, n_bins)``, i.e. the\n   258\t    right edge of each spike bin.\n   259\t\n   260\t    Returns\n   261\t    -------\n   262\t    vals : (n_intervals, n_bins) float array (rows of NaN where invalid)\n   263\t    good : (n_intervals,) bool array\n   264\t    reasons : list of str or None, per interval\n   265\t    \"\"\"\n   266\t    interval_ends = interval_begs + n_bins * binsize\n   267\t    idxs_beg = np.searchsorted(times, interval_begs, side='right')\n   268\t    idxs_end = np.searchsorted(times, interval_ends, side='left')\n   269\t\n   270\t    n = len(interval_begs)\n   271\t    vals = np.full((n, n_bins), np.nan, dtype=np.float64)\n   272\t    good = np.zeros(n, dtype=bool)\n   273\t    reasons = [None] * n\n   274\t\n   275\t    for k in range(n):\n   276\t        t = times[idxs_beg[k]:idxs_end[k]]\n   277\t        v = values[idxs_beg[k]:idxs_end[k]]\n   278\t        if len(v) == 0:\n   279\t            reasons[k] = 'target data not present'\n   280\t            continue\n   281\t        if np.isnan(interval_begs[k]) or np.isnan(interval_ends[k]):\n   282\t            reasons[k] = 'bad interval data'\n   283\t            continue\n   284\t        if np.abs(interval_begs[k] - t[0]) > binsize:\n   285\t            reasons[k] = 'target data starts too late'\n   286\t            continue\n   287\t        if np.abs(interval_ends[k] - t[-1]) > binsize:\n   288\t            reasons[k] = 'target data ends too early'\n   289\t            continue\n   290\t        if np.any(np.isnan(v)):\n   291\t            # the reference keeps these (allow_nans=True) and imputes the trial\n   292\t            # mean inside its data loader; a categorical target cannot be\n   293\t            # imputed without inventing a class, so the trial is dropped\n   294\t            reasons[k] = 'nans in target data'\n   295\t            continue\n   296\t        x = np.linspace(interval_begs[k] + binsize, interval_ends[k], n_bins)\n   297\t        vals[k] = interp1d(t, v, kind='linear', fill_value='extrapolate')(x)\n   298\t        good[k] = True\n   299\t    return vals, good, reasons\n   300\t\n   301\t\n   302\tdef discretize_tertiles(values):\n   303\t    \"\"\"Map a (n_trials, n_bins) continuous array onto {0, 1, 2} by tertile.\n   304\t\n   305\t    Thresholds are the 33.3 / 66.7 percentiles of all values pooled over the\n   306\t    session's retained trials, so each session's classes are balanced and the\n   307\t    arbitrary units of motion energy do not have to be comparable across\n   308\t    sessions.\n   309\t    \"\"\"\n   310\t    flat = values.reshape(-1)\n   311\t    q1, q2 = np.quantile(flat, TERTILES)\n   312\t    if not (q1 < q2):\n   313\t        # degenerate (heavily tied) distribution: fall back to the distinct\n   314\t        # quantile values that do exist so the labels stay monotone\n   315\t        edges = np.unique([q1, q2])\n   316\t        labels = np.digitize(values, edges, right=False)\n   317\t        return labels.astype(np.int64), (float(q1), float(q2))\n   318\t    labels = np.digitize(values, [q1, q2], right=False).astype(np.int64)\n   319\t    return labels, (float(q1), float(q2))\n   320\t\n   321\t\n   322\tdef trial_number_in_block(probability_left):\n   323\t    \"\"\"0-based index of each trial within its constant-``probabilityLeft`` block.\n   324\t\n   325\t    Computed on the *unfiltered* trials table, because the block structure is a\n   326\t    property of the experiment, not of which trials survive curation.\n   327\t    \"\"\"\n   328\t    p = np.asarray(probability_left, dtype=float)\n   329\t    # a change (including to/from NaN) starts a new block\n   330\t    changed = np.ones(len(p), dtype=bool)\n   331\t    if len(p) > 1:\n   332\t        same = (p[1:] == p[:-1]) | (np.isnan(p[1:]) & np.isnan(p[:-1]))\n   333\t        changed[1:] = ~same\n   334\t    block_id = np.cumsum(changed) - 1\n   335\t    # index within block = position - position of first trial of that block\n   336\t    first_of_block = np.zeros(block_id[-1] + 1, dtype=np.int64)\n   337\t    starts = np.nonzero(changed)[0]\n   338\t    first_of_block[:] = starts\n   339\t    return np.arange(len(p)) - first_of_block[block_id]\n   340\t\n   341\t\n   342\t# \"\"\"Trials whose window is spanned by this stream, allowing the one bin gap the reference allows.\"\"\"\n   170\t    start, stop = stim_on + T_START, stim_on + T_STOP\n   171\t    begin =    \\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\n    Select spiking data for specified interval in each recording.\\\\n\\\\n    Parameters\\\\n    ----------\\\\n    times : array-like\\\\n        time in seconds for \\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\"\\\\n    n_intervals = len(interval_begs)\\\\n\\\\n    # np.ceil because we want to make sure our bins contain all data\\\\n    n_bins = int(np.ceil(interval_len / \"content\": \"1\\tFrom \\\"Exploiting correlations across trials and behavioral sessions to improve neural decoding\\\"\\n2\\t\\n3\\tOur goal is to decode behavior y \\\\in R^P from spike-sorted, temporally binned spike counts. For each trial k, neural activity has size N x T, where N is the number of neurons and T the number of time steps. Recordings are split into 2-s trials, each divided into 20-ms bins, producing T = 100 time steps. For each trial, we constructed X \\\\in R^{N x T}  by aggregating spike counts and used it to compute a decoder estimate of the true behavior y \\\\in R^P. y is constant within a trial (“per-trial decoding”); when P = T, y varies across time (“per-timestep decoding”).\\n4\\t\\n5\\tWe apply our models to 433 IBL sessions,17 covering 270 brain regions and four behavioral variables: choice, prior, wheel speed, and whisker motion energy.\\n6\\t\\n7\\t In the IBL experiments, mice rotate a wheel to indicate the location of a visual stimulus, defined as their choice (Figure 1A). For the first 90 trials, the stimulus appears randomly on either side with equal probability; in subsequent trials, it appears predominantly on one side in blocks. Mice adapt their behavior to these changing probabilities, allowing estimation of each mouse’s trial-by-trial prior belief (prior) about stimulus location. Additionally, wheel speed and whisker motion energy near the whisker pad are recorded. Whisker motion energy is computed as the mean absolute difference between adjacent video frames within a bounding box anchored between nose tip and eye. Choice and prior are static within a trial, while wheel speed and whisker motion energy are time-varying signals sampled at 60 Hz. See STAR Methods sections “data processing” and “hyperparameter selection” for details.\\n8\\t\\n9\\tData processing\\n10\\t\\n11\\tIBL trial-aligned dataset\\n12\\t\\n13\\tFor choice, we align trials to the stimulus onset, considering neural activity from 0.5 s before to 1.5 s post-onset. For prior, we also align trials to the stimulus onset, including neural activity from 0.6 s to 0.1 s pre-onset. The prior represents the mice’s estimate of the stimulus side probability. We use the same decoding window as in the previous study,27 focusing on the period with minimal wheel movements. Within each trial, we segment neural activity into 50-ms non-overlapping time bins. For each time bin, we bin spike counts using all neurons, sorted by Kilosort 2.5,77 from each session. For dynamic behaviors (wheel speed and whisker motion energy), we select the first movement onset as the alignment event, and decode the behavior starting at the alignment event and ending at 1 s after the alignment event. The neural activity within each trial is binned into non-overlapping 20 ms bins. For each time bin, we similarly bin spike counts using all neurons from each session.\\n14\\t\\n15\\tIBL trial-unaligned dataset\\n16\\t\\n17\\tWe focus only on wheel speed and whisker motion energy, as variables like choice and prior are only defined during experimental trials, which are periods when stimuli are presented and mice respond for rewards. Unlike the trial-aligned dataset, we do not align neural activity and behavior to a specific event onset. Instead, we segment the continuous Neuropixels recordings into 2-s snippets to construct the trial-unaligned dataset for each session. These snippets cover intervals both during and outside experimental trials, capturing the repetitive, structured behaviors within trials as well as the more spontaneous behaviors outside of trials.\\n18\\t\\n19\\tFrom \\\"A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour\\\"\\n20\\t\\n21\\tWe trained 139 mice (94 male and 45 female) on the International Brain Laboratory (IBL) decision-making task (Fig. 1a,b). On each trial, a visual stimulus appeared to the left or right on a screen, and the mouse had to move it to the centre by turning a wheel with its front paws within 60 s (Fig. 1c). After an initial 90 unbiased trials, the prior probability for the stimulus to appear on the left or right side was constant over a block of trials at a ratio of 20:80% (right block) or 80:20% (left block). Blocks lasted for between 20 and 100 trials, which were drawn from a truncated geometric distribution (empirical mean of 51 trials). Block changes were not cued. Stimulus contrast was uniformly sampled from 5 possible values (100, 25, 12.5, 6.25 and 0%). The 0% contrast trials, when no stimulus was presented, were assigned to a left or right side following the probability distribution of the block. This allowed mice to perform above chance by incorporating this prior in their choices. Following a wheel turn, mice received positive feedback in the form of a water reward, or negative feedback in the form of a white-noise pulse and a 2-s time out. The next trial began after a delay, followed by a quiescence period during which the mice had to hold the wheel still.\\n22\\t\\n23\\tRecordings\\n24\\t\\n25\\tIn these mice, we inserted 699 Neuropixels probes (see an example of one recording of three trials in Fig. 1i), following a grid that covered the left hemisphere of the forebrain and midbrain, which typically represent stimuli or actions on the contralateral side, and the right hemisphere of the cerebellum and hindbrain, which typically represent the ipsilateral side (Fig. 2a). Recordings were collected by 12 laboratories in Europe and the USA, with most recordings using 2 simultaneous probe insertions. To ensure reproducibility, one brain location was targeted in every mouse in every laboratory, as described elsewhere25. Only sessions with at least 400 trials were retained for further analyses. Data were uploaded to a central server, preprocessed and shared through a standardized interface. To perform spike sorting on the recordings, we used a version of Kilosort with custom additions. This process produced 621,733 units (including multineuron activity), averaging 889 per probe. To separate individual neurons from clusters of multineuron activity, we then applied stringent quality-control metrics (based on those described in ref. 15), which identified 75,708 well-isolated neurons, averaging 108 per probe.\\n26\\t\\n27\\tMethods\\n28\\t\\n29\\tn brief, at the beginning of each trial, the mouse was required to not move the wheel for a quiescence period of 400–700 ms. After the quiescence period, a visual stimulus (Gabor patch) appeared on either the left or right (±35° azimuth) of the screen, with a contrast randomly sampled from a predefined set (100, 25, 12.5, 6 or 0%). A 100-ms tone (5-kHz sine wave) was played at stimulus onset. Mice had 60 s to move the wheel and make a response. Stimuli were yoked to the rotation of the response wheel, such that a 1-mm movement of the wheel moved the stimulus by 4 visual degrees. A response was registered if the centre of the stimulus crossed the  ±35° azimuth line from its original position. If the mouse correctly moved the stimulus 35° to the centre of the screen, it immediately received a 3-μl reward; if it incorrectly moved the stimulus 35° away from the centre, it received a time out. If the mouse responded incorrectly or failed to reach either threshold within the 60-s window, a white-noise burst was played for 500 ms and the inter-trial interval was between 1 and 1.5 s. In trials for which the visual stimulus contrast was set to 0%, the mouse had to respond as for any other trial by turning the wheel in the correct direction (assigned according to the statistics of the prevailing block) to receive a reward, but the mouse was not able to perceive whether the stimulus was presented on the left or right side of the screen. The mouse also received feedback (noise burst or reward) on 0% contrast trials.\\n30\\t\\n31\\tEach session started with 90 trials in which the probability of a visual stimulus appearing on the left or right side was equal. Specifically, the 100%, 25%, 12.5% and 6% contrast trials were each presented 10 times on each side, and the 0% contrast was presented 10 times in total (that is, the ratio of the 100, 25, 12.5, 6 and 0% contrasts were set at 2, 2, 2, 2 and 1, respectively). The side (and thus correct movement) for the 0% contrast trials was chosen randomly between the right and left with equal probability. This initial block of 90 trials is referred to as the unbiased block (50:50).\\n32\\t\\n33\\tAfter the unbiased block, trials were presented in biased blocks: in right-bias blocks, stimuli appeared on the right on 80% of the trials, whereas in left-bias blocks, stimuli appeared on the right on 20% of the trials. The ratio of the contrasts remained as above (2:2:2:2:1). Whether the first biased block in a session was left or right was randomly chosen, and blocks were then alternated. The length of a block was drawn from an exponential distribution with scale parameter of 60 trials, but truncated to lie between 20 and 100 trials.\\n34\\t\\n35\\tThe automated shaping protocol for training involved two collections of sessions. In the first session, the animals started performing a version of the task without biased blocks and were then progressively introduced to harder stimuli with weaker contrasts as they became progressively more competent. They also experienced a debiasing protocol, which was intended to dissuade them from persisting with just one of the choices. Once they were performing sufficiently well on all non-zero contrasts, they were faced with the biased blocks. When, in turn, performance on those was adequate (including on 0% contrast trials, which are informed by the block), they graduated to recording. Supplementary Figure 8a shows a joint histogram of the number of sessions the mice took in the first and second collections (these were not correlated). Supplementary Figure 8b shows a joint histogram of the number of sessions the mice took in the second collection and the performance during the recording sessions. These were also not correlated.\\n36\\t\\n37\\tInclusion criteria\\n38\\t\\n39\\tWe applied a set of inclusion criteria to sessions, probes and neurons to ensure data quality. Supplementary Table 1 lists the consequences of these criteria for the number of sessions and probes that passed the criteria.\\n40\\tSessions and insertions\\n41\\t\\n42\\tEach Neuropixels insertion was repeated in at least two laboratories, with reproducibility of outcomes across laboratories verified with extensive analyses that we have previously reported25.\\n43\\t\\n44\\tSessions were included in the data release if the mice performed at least 250 trials, with a performance of at least 90% correct on 100% contrast trials for both left and right blocks, and, to be able to analyse the feedback variable, if there were at least 3 trials with incorrect choices (after applying the trial exclusions below). Furthermore, sessions were included in the release only if they reached threshold on a collection of hardware tests (definitions are available from GiHub (https://int-brain-lab.github.io/iblenv/_autosummary/ibllib.qc.task_metrics.html)).\\n45\\t\\n46\\tInsertions were excluded if the neural data failed the whole recording per visually assessed criteria of the ‘Recording Inclusion metrics and Guidelines for Optimal Reproducibility’ (RIGOR) from ref. 25, by presenting major artefacts (see examples in ref. 28) or if the probe tract could not be recovered during the histology procedure. Furthermore, only insertions for which alignments had been resolved (see appendix 6 of ref. 25 for definitions) were used in this study.\\n47\\t\\n48\\tAfter applying these criteria, a total of 459 sessions, 699 insertions and 621,733 neurons remained, constituting the publicly released dataset.\\n49\\tTrials\\n50\\t\\n51\\tFor the analyses presented here, trials were excluded if one of the following trial events could not be detected: choice, probabilityLeft, feebackType, feeback times, stimON times and firstMovement times. Trials were further excluded if the time between stimulus onset and the first movement of the wheel (the first wheel-movement time) were outside the range of 0.08–2.00 s.\\n52\\tNeurons and brain regions\\n53\\t\\n54\\tNeurons generated by the spike-sorting pipeline were excluded from the analyses presented here if they failed one of the three criteria described in ref. 28 (the single unit computed metrics of RIGOR25): amplitude > 50 μV; noise cut-off < 20 μV; and refractory period violation. Neurons that passed these criteria were termed well-isolated neurons (or often just ‘neurons’) in this study. Out of the 621,733 units collected, 75,708 were considered well-isolated neurons. Final analyses were additionally restricted to regions that were designated grey matter in the adult mouse Allen Common Coordinate framework6, contained at least five well-isolated neurons per session and were recorded from in at least two such sessions.\\n55\\t\\n56\\tVideo analysis\\n57\\t\\n58\\tWe briefly describe the video analysis pipeline (full details can be found in ref. 105). The recording rigs contained three cameras: one called ‘left’ at full resolution (1,280 × 1,024) and 60 Hz, filming the mouse from one side; one called ‘right’, filming the mouse symmetrically from the other side at half resolution (640 × 512) and 150 Hz; and one called ‘body’ at half resolution and 30 Hz, filming the body of the mouse from above. We developed several quality-control metrics to detect raw video issues such as poor illumination (as infrared light bulbs broke) or accidental misplacement of the cameras105.\\n59\\t\\n60\\tWe computed the motion energy (the mean across pixels of the absolute value of the difference between adjacent frames) of the whisker pad areas in the ‘left’ and ‘right’ videos (Fig. 1d). The whisker pad area was empirically defined using a rectangular bounding box anchored between the nose tip and the eye, both found using DeepLabCut106 (DLC; see more below). This metric quantifies motion in the whisker pad area and has a temporal resolution of the respective camera.\\n61\\t\\n62\\tWe also performed markerless pose estimation of body parts using DLC31, which is used in a fully automated pipeline in IBL (v.2.1) to track various body parts such as the paws, nose, tongue and pupil (Fig. 1d). In all analyses using DLC estimates, we excluded predictions with likelihood < 0.9. Furthermore, we developed several quality-control metrics for the DLC traces105.\\n63\\t\\n64\\tOverview of decoding\\n65\\t\\n66\\tWe performed a decoding analysis to measure how much information the activity of populations of neurons contained about task variables such as stimulus side and choice. To do this we, used cross-validated, maximum-likelihood regression with L1 regularization (to zero out the contribution from noisy neurons). The neural regressors were defined by binning the spike counts from each neuron in each session in a given region in a specific time window on each trial. The duration of the time window, the number of bins in that time window (that is, the bin size) and the trial event to which it was aligned depended on the variable that is the target of our regression (Supplementary Table 2). These factors are discussed further below and include a variety of behavioural and task variables: stimulus side, choice, feedback and wheel speed and velocity. Although a session may have included multiple probe insertions, we did not perform decoding on these probes separately because they are not independent. Instead, neurons in the same session and region were combined across probes for our decoding analysis. Decoding was cross-validated and compared with a null distribution to test for significance. A given region may have been recorded on multiple sessions; therefore, in the main figures (Figs. 4–7) the region P value was defined by combining session P values using Fisher’s combined probability test, and the region effect size was defined by subtracting the median of the null distribution from the decoding score and reporting the median of the resulting values across sessions. The P values for all regions were then subjected to FDR correction for multiple comparisons at q = 0.01.\\n67\\t\\n68\\tDecoding target variables\\n69\\t\\n70\\tStimulus side, choice and feedback were treated as binary target variables for logistic regression. For stimulus side, trials that had zero contrast were excluded. We used the LogisticRegression module from scikit-learn111 (v.1.1.2) with 0.001 tolerance, 20,000 maximum iterations, “l1” penalty, “liblinear” solver and “fit_intercept” set to True. We balanced decoder classes by weighting samples by the inverse of the class frequency, 1/(2Pi,class). Decoding performance was evaluated using the balanced accuracy of classification, which is the average of the recall probabilities for the two classes. Supplementary Figure 9 shows histograms of the regression coefficients for all the variables.\\n71\\t\\n72\\tWheel values (speed and velocity) change over the course of a trial, unlike the previous decoding targets, and we therefore had to treat these target variables differently. We averaged wheel values in nonoverlapping 20-ms bins, starting 200 ms before first wheel-movement time and ending at 1,000 ms after first wheel-movement time. Spike counts were similarly binned. The target value for a given bin (ending at time t) was decoded from spikes in a preceding (causal) window spanning W bins (ending at times t, …, t-W). Therefore, if decoding from n neurons, there were (W + 1)n predictors of the target variable in a given bin. In practice, we used W = 10. To decode these continuous-valued targets, we performed linear regression using the Lasso module from scikit-learn111 (v.1.1.2) with 0.001 tolerance, 1,000 maximum iterations and “fit_intercept” set to True. Decoding performance was evaluated using the R2 metric.\\n73\\n\\n[metadata] {\\\"type\\\": \\\"text\\\", \\\"file\\\": {\\\"filePath\\\": \\\"/app/methods.txt\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"From \\\\\\\"Exploiting correlations across trials and behavioral sessions to improve neural decoding\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\nOur goal is to decode behavior y \\\\\\\\in R^P from spike-sorted, temporally binned spike counts. For each trial k, neural activity has size N x T, where N is the number of neurons and T the number of time steps. Recordings are split into 2-s trials, each divided into 20-ms bins, producing T = 100 time steps. For each trial, we constructed X \\\\\\\\in R^{N x T}  by aggregating spike counts and used it to compute a decoder estimate of the true behavior y \\\\\\\\in R^P. y is constant within a trial (“per-trial decoding”); when P = T, y varies across time (“per-timestep decoding”).\\\\n\\\\nWe apply our models to 433 IBL sessions,17 covering 270 brain regions and four behavioral variables: choice, prior, wheel speed, and whisker motion energy.\\\\n\\\\n In the IBL experiments, mice rotate a wheel to indicate the location of a visual stimulus, defined as their choice (Figure 1A). For the first 90 trials, the stimulus appears randomly on either side with equal probability; in subsequent trials, it appears predominantly on one side in blocks. Mice adapt their behavior to these changing probabilities, allowing estimation of each mouse’s trial-by-trial prior belief (prior) about stimulus location. Additionally, wheel speed and whisker motion energy near the whisker pad are recorded. Whisker motion energy is computed as the mean absolute difference between adjacent video frames within a bounding box anchored between nose tip and eye. Choice and prior are static within a trial, while wheel speed and whisker motion energy are time-varying signals sampled at 60 Hz. See STAR Methods sections “data processing” and “hyperparameter selection” for details.\\\\n\\\\nData processing\\\\n\\\\nIBL trial-aligned dataset\\\\n\\\\nFor choice, we align trials to the stimulus onset, considering neural activity from 0.5 s before to 1.5 s post-onset. For prior, we also align trials to the stimulus onset, including neural activity from 0.6 s to 0.1 s pre-onset. The prior represents the mice’s estimate of the stimulus side probability. We use the same decoding window as in the previous study,27 focusing on the period with minimal wheel movements. Within each trial, we segment neural activity into 50-ms non-overlapping time bins. For each time bin, we bin spike counts using all neurons, sorted by Kilosort 2.5,77 from each session. For dynamic behaviors (wheel speed and whisker motion energy), we select the first movement onset as the alignment event, and decode the behavior starting at the alignment event and ending at 1 s after the alignment event. The neural activity within each trial is binned into non-overlapping 20 ms bins. For each time bin, we similarly bin spike counts using all neurons from each session.\\\\n\\\\nIBL trial-unaligned dataset\\\\n\\\\nWe focus only on wheel speed and whisker motion energy, as variables like choice and prior are only defined during experimental trials, which are periods when stimuli are presented and mice respond for rewards. Unlike the trial-aligned dataset, we do not align neural activity and behavior to a specific event onset. Instead, we segment the continuous Neuropixels recordings into 2-s snippets to construct the trial-unaligned dataset for each session. These snippets cover intervals both during and outside experimental trials, capturing the repetitive, structured behaviors within trials as well as the more spontaneous behaviors outside of trials.\\\\n\\\\nFrom \\\\\\\"A brain-wide map of neural activity during complex behaviour\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\nWe trained 139 mice (94 male and 45 female) on the International Brain Laboratory (IBL) decision-making task (Fig. 1a,b). On each trial, a visual stimulus appeared to the left or right on a screen, and the mouse had to move it to the centre by turning a wheel with its front paws within 60 s (Fig. 1c). After an initial 90 unbiased trials, the prior probability for the stimulus to appear on the left or right side was constant over a block of trials at a ratio of 20:80% (right block) or 80:20% (left block). Blocks lasted for between 20 and 100 trials, which were drawn from a truncated geometric distribution (empirical mean of 51 trials). Block changes were not cued. Stimulus contrast was uniformly sampled from 5 possible values (100, 25, 12.5, 6.25 and 0%). The 0% contrast trials, when no stimulus was presented, were assigned to a left or right side following the probability distribution of the block. This allowed mice to perform above chance by incorporating this prior in their choices. Following a wheel turn, mice received positive feedback in the form of a water reward, or negative feedback in the form of a white-noise pulse and a 2-s time out. The next trial began after a delay, followed by a quiescence period during which the mice had to hold the wheel still.\\\\n\\\\nRecordings\\\\n\\\\nIn these mice, we inserted 699 Neuropixels probes (see an example of one recording of three trials in Fig. 1i), following a grid that covered the left hemisphere of the forebrain and midbrain, which typically represent stimuli or actions on the contralateral side, and the right hemisphere of the cerebellum and hindbrain, which typically represent the ipsilateral side (Fig. 2a). Recordings were collected by 12 laboratories in Europe and the USA, with most recordings using 2 simultaneous probe insertions. To ensure reproducibility, one brain location was targeted in every mouse in every laboratory, as described elsewhere25. Only sessions with at least 400 trials were retained for further analyses. Data were uploaded to a central server, preprocessed and shared through a standardized interface. To perform spike sorting on the recordings, we used a version of Kilosort with custom additions. This process produced 621,733 units (including multineuron activity), averaging 889 per probe. To separate individual neurons from clusters of multineuron activity, we then applied stringent quality-control metrics (based on those described in ref. 15), which identified 75,708 well-isolated neurons, averaging 108 per probe.\\\\n\\\\nMethods\\\\n\\\\nn brief, at the beginning of each trial, the mouse was required to not move the wheel for a quiescence period of 400–700 ms. After the quiescence period, a visual stimulus (Gabor patch) appeared on either the left or right (±35° azimuth) of the screen, with a contrast randomly sampled from a predefined set (100, 25, 12.5, 6 or 0%). A 100-ms tone (5-kHz sine wave) was played at stimulus onset. Mice had 60 s to move the wheel and make a response. Stimuli were yoked to the rotation of the response wheel, such that a 1-mm movement of the wheel moved the stimulus by 4 visual degrees. A response was registered if the centre of the stimulus crossed the  ±35° azimuth line from its original position. If the mouse correctly moved the stimulus 35° to the centre of the screen, it immediately received a 3-μl reward; if it incorrectly moved the stimulus 35° away from the centre, it received a time out. If the mouse responded incorrectly or failed to reach either threshold within the 60-s window, a white-noise burst was played for 500 ms and the inter-trial interval was between 1 and 1.5 s. In trials for which the visual stimulus contrast was set to 0%, the mouse had to respond as for any other trial by turning the wheel in the correct direction (assigned according to the statistics of the prevailing block) to receive a reward, but the mouse was not able to perceive whether the stimulus was presented on the left or right side of the screen. The mouse also received feedback (noise burst or reward) on 0% contrast trials.\\\\n\\\\nEach session started with 90 trials in which the probability of a visual stimulus appearing on the left or right side was equal. Specifically, the 100%, 25%, 12.5% and 6% contrast trials were each presented 10 times on each side, and the 0% contrast was presented 10 times in total (that is, the ratio of the 100, 25, 12.5, 6 and 0% contrasts were set at 2, 2, 2, 2 and 1, respectively). The side (and thus correct movement) for the 0% contrast trials was chosen randomly between the right and left with equal probability. This initial block of 90 trials is referred to as the unbiased block (50:50).\\\\n\\\\nAfter the unbiased block, trials were presented in biased blocks: in right-bias blocks, stimuli appeared on the right on 80% of the trials, whereas in left-bias blocks, stimuli appeared on the right on 20% of the trials. The ratio of the contrasts remained as above (2:2:2:2:1). Whether the first biased block in a session was left or right was randomly chosen, and blocks were then alternated. The length of a block was drawn from an exponential distribution with scale parameter of 60 trials, but truncated to lie between 20 and 100 trials.\\\\n\\\\nThe automated shaping protocol for training involved two collections of sessions. In the first session, the animals started performing a version of the task without biased blocks and were then progressively introduced to harder stimuli with weaker contrasts as they became progressively more competent. They also experienced a debiasing protocol, which was intended to dissuade them from persisting with just one of the choices. Once they were performing sufficiently well on all non-zero contrasts, they were faced with the biased blocks. When, in turn, performance on those was adequate (including on 0% contrast trials, which are informed by the block), they graduated to recording. Supplementary Figure 8a shows a joint histogram of the number of sessions the mice took in the first and second collections (these were not correlated). Supplementary Figure 8b shows a joint histogram of the number of sessions the mice took in the second collection and the performance during the recording sessions. These were also not correlated.\\\\n\\\\nInclusion criteria\\\\n\\\\nWe applied a set of inclusion criteria to sessions, probes and neurons to ensure data quality. Supplementary Table 1 lists the consequences of these criteria for the number of sessions and probes that passed the criteria.\\\\nSessions and insertions\\\\n\\\\nEach Neuropixels insertion was repeated in at least two laboratories, with reproducibility of outcomes across laboratories verified with extensive analyses that we have previously reported25.\\\\n\\\\nSessions were included in the data release if the mice performed at least 250 trials, with a performance of at least 90% correct on 100% contrast trials for both left and right blocks, and, to be able to analyse the feedback variable, if there were at least 3 trials with incorrect choices (after applying the trial exclusions below). Furthermore, sessions were included in the release only if they reached threshold on a collection of hardware tests (definitions are available from GiHub (https://int-brain-lab.github.io/iblenv/_autosummary/ibllib.qc.task_metrics.html)).\\\\n\\\\nInsertions were excluded if the neural data failed the whole recording per visually assessed criteria of the ‘Recording Inclusion metrics and Guidelines for Optimal Reproducibility’ (RIGOR) from ref. 25, by presenting major artefacts (see examples in ref. 28) or if the probe tract could not be recovered during the histology procedure. Furthermore, only insertions for which alignments had been resolved (see appendix 6 of ref. 25 for definitions) were used in this study.\\\\n\\\\nAfter applying these criteria, a total of 459 sessions, 699 insertions and 621,733 neurons remained, constituting the publicly released dataset.\\\\nTrials\\\\n\\\\nFor the analyses presented here, trials were excluded if one of the following trial events could not be detected: choice, probabilityLeft, feebackType, feeback times, stimON times and firstMovement times. Trials were further excluded if the time between stimulus onset and the first movement of the wheel (the first wheel-movement time) were outside the range of 0.08–2.00 s.\\\\nNeurons and brain regions\\\\n\\\\nNeurons generated by the spike-sorting pipeline were excluded from the analyses presented here if they failed one of the three criteria described in ref. 28 (the single unit computed metrics of RIGOR25): amplitude > 50 μV; noise cut-off < 20 μV; and refractory period violation. Neurons that passed these criteria were termed well-isolated neurons (or often just ‘neurons’) in this study. Out of the 621,733 units collected, 75,708 were considered well-isolated neurons. Final analyses were additionally restricted to regions that were designated grey matter in the adult mouse Allen Common Coordinate framework6, contained at least five well-isolated neurons per session and were recorded from in at least two such sessions.\\\\n\\\\nVideo analysis\\\\n\\\\nWe briefly describe the video analysis pipeline (full details can be found in ref. 105). The recording rigs contained three cameras: one called ‘left’ at full resolution (1,280 × 1,024) and 60 Hz, filming the mouse from one side; one called ‘right’, filming the mouse symmetrically from the other side at half resolution (640 × 512) and 150 Hz; and one called ‘body’ at half resolution and 30 Hz, filming the body of the mouse from above. We developed several quality-control metrics to detect raw video issues such as poor illumination (as infrared light bulbs broke) or accidental misplacement of the cameras105.\\\\n\\\\nWe computed the motion energy (the mean across pixels of the absolute value of the difference between adjacent frames) of the whisker pad areas in the ‘left’ and ‘right’ videos (Fig. 1d). The whisker pad area was empirically defined using a rectangular bounding box anchored between the nose tip and the eye, both found using DeepLabCut106 (DLC; see more below). This metric quantifies motion in the whisker pad area and has a temporal resolution of the respective camera.\\\\n\\\\nWe also performed markerless pose estimation of body parts using DLC31, which is used in a fully automated pipeline in IBL (v.2.1) to track various body parts such as the paws, nose, tongue and pupil (Fig. 1d). In all analyses using DLC estimates, we excluded predictions with likelihood < 0.9. Furthermore, we developed several quality-control metrics for the DLC traces105.\\\\n\\\\nOverview of decoding\\\\n\\\\nWe performed a decoding analysis to measure how much information the activity of populations of neurons contained about task variables such as stimulus side and choice. To do this we, used cross-validated, maximum-likelihood regression with L1 regularization (to zero out the contribution from noisy neurons). The neural regressors were defined by binning the spike counts from each neuron in each session in a given region in a specific time window on each trial. The duration of the time window, the number of bins in that time window (that is, the bin size) and the trial event to which it was aligned depended on the variable that is the target of our regression (Supplementary Table 2). These factors are discussed further below and include a variety of behavioural and task variables: stimulus side, choice, feedback and wheel speed and velocity. Although a session may have included multiple probe insertions, we did not perform decoding on these probes separately because they are not independent. Instead, neurons in the same session and region were combined across probes for our decoding analysis. Decoding was cross-validated and compared with a null distribution to test for significance. A given region may have been recorded on multiple sessions; therefore, in the main figures (Figs. 4–7) the region P value was defined by combining session P values using Fisher’s combined probability test, and the region effect size was defined by subtracting the median of the null distribution from the decoding score and reporting the median of the resulting values across sessions. The P values for all regions were then subjected to FDR correction for multiple comparisons at q = 0.01.\\\\n\\\\nDecoding target variables\\\\n\\\\nStimulus side, choice and feedback were treated as binary target variables for logistic regression. For stimulus side, trials that had zero contrast were excluded. We used the LogisticRegression module from scikit-learn111 (v.1.1.2) with 0.001 tolerance, 20,000 maximum iterations, “l1” penalty, “liblinear” solver and “fit_intercept” set to True. We balanced decoder classes by weighting samples by the inverse of the class frequency, 1/(2Pi,class). Decoding performance was evaluated using the balanced accuracy of classification, which is the average of the recall probabilities for the two classes. Supplementary Figure 9 shows histograms of the regression coefficients for all the variables.\\\\n\\\\nWheel values (speed and velocity) change over the course of a trial, unlike the previous decoding targets, and we therefore had to treat these target variables differently. We averaged wheel values in nonoverlapping 20-ms bins, starting 200 ms before first wheel-movement time and ending at 1,000 ms after first wheel-movement time. Spike counts were similarly binned. The target value for a given bin (ending at time t) was decoded from spikes in a preceding (causal) window spanning W bins (ending at times t, …, t-W). Therefore, if decoding from n neurons, there were (W + 1)n predictors of the target variable in a given bin. In practice, we used W = 10. To decode these continuous-valued targets, we performed linear regression using the Lasso module from scikit-learn111 (v.1.1.2) with 0.001 tolerance, 1,000 maximum iterations and “fit_intercept” set to True. For each trial k, neural activity has size N x T, where N is the number of neurons and T the number of time steps. Recordings are split into 2-s trials, each divided into 20-ms bins, producing T = 100 time steps. For each trial, we constructed X \\\\in R^{N x T}  by aggregating spike counts and used it to compute a decoder estimate of the true behavior y \\\\in R^P. y is constant within a trial (“per-trial decoding”); when P = T, y varies across time (“per-timestep decoding”).\\n4\\t\\n5\\tWe apply our models to 433 IBL sessions,17 covering 270 brain regions and four behavioral variables: choice, prior, wheel speed, and whisker motion energy.\\n6\\t\\n7\\t In the IBL experiments, mice rotate a wheel to indicate the location of a visual stimulus, defined as their choice (Figure 1A). Mice adapt their behavior to these changing probabilities, allowing estimation of each mouse’s trial-by-trial prior belief (prior) about stimulus location. Additionally, wheel speed and whisker motion energy near the whisker pad are recorded. Whisker motion energy is computed as the mean absolute difference between adjacent video frames within a bounding box anchored between nose tip and eye. Choice and prior are static within a trial, while wheel speed and whisker motion energy are time-varying signals sampled at 60 Hz. See STAR Methods sections “data processing” and “hyperparameter selection” for details.\\n8\\t\\n9\\tData processing\\n10\\t\\n11\\tIBL trial-aligned dataset\\n12\\t\\n13\\tFor choice, we align trials to the stimulus onset, considering neural activity from 0.5 s before to 1.5 s post-onset. For prior, we also align trials to the stimulus onset, including neural activity from 0.6 s to 0.1 s pre-onset. The prior represents the mice’s estimate of the stimulus side probability. We use the same decoding window as in the previous study,27 focusing on the period with minimal wheel movements. Within each trial, we segment neural activity into 50-ms non-overlapping time bins. For each time bin, we bin spike counts using all neurons, sorted by Kilosort 2.5,77 from each session. For dynamic behaviors (wheel speed and whisker motion energy), we select the first movement onset as the alignment event, and decode the behavior starting at the alignment event and ending at 1 s after the alignment event. On each trial, a visual stimulus appeared to the left or right on a screen, and the mouse had to move it to the centre by turning a wheel with its front paws within 60 s (Fig. 1c). After an initial 90 unbiased trials, the prior probability for the stimulus to appear on the left or right side was constant over a block of trials at a ratio of 20:80% (right block) or 80:20% (left block). Blocks lasted for between 20 and 100 trials, which were drawn from a truncated geometric distribution (empirical mean of 51 trials). Block changes were not cued. Stimulus contrast was uniformly sampled from 5 possible values (100, 25, 12.5, 6.25 and 0%). The 0% contrast trials, when no stimulus was presented, were assigned to a left or right side following the probability distribution of the block. This allowed mice to perform above chance by incorporating this prior in their choices. Following a wheel turn, mice received positive feedback in the form of a water reward, or negative feedback in the form of a white-noise pulse and a 2-s time out. The next trial began after a delay, followed by a quiescence period during which the mice had to hold the wheel still.\\n22\\t\\n23\\tRecordings\\n24\\t\\n25\\tIn these mice, we inserted 699 Neuropixels probes (see an example of one recording of three trials in Fig. 1i), following a grid that covered the left hemisphere of the forebrain and midbrain, which typically represent stimuli or actions on the contralateral side, and the right hemisphere of the cerebellum and hindbrain, which typically represent the ipsilateral side (Fig. 2a). Recordings were collected by 12 laboratories in Europe and the USA, with most recordings using 2 simultaneous probe insertions. To ensure reproducibility, one brain location was targeted in every mouse in every laboratory, as described elsewhere25. Only sessions with at least 400 trials were retained for further analyses. Data were uploaded to a central server, preprocessed and shared through a standardized interface. To perform spike sorting on the recordings, we used a version of Kilosort with custom additions. This process produced 621,733 units (including multineuron activity), averaging 889 per probe. To separate individual neurons from clusters of multineuron activity, we then applied stringent quality-control metrics (based on those described in ref. 15), which identified 75,708 well-isolated neurons, averaging 108 per probe.\\n26\\t\\n27\\tMethods\\n28\\t\\n29\\tn brief, at the beginning of each trial, the mouse was required to not move the wheel for a quiescence period of 400–700 ms. After the quiescence period, a visual stimulus (Gabor patch) appeared on either the left or right (±35° azimuth) of the screen, with a contrast randomly sampled from a predefined set (100, 25, 12.5, 6 or 0%). A 100-ms tone (5-kHz sine wave) was played at stimulus onset. Mice had 60 s to move the wheel and make a response. Stimuli were yoked to the rotation of the response wheel, such that a 1-mm movement of the wheel moved the stimulus by 4 visual degrees. A response was registered if the centre of the stimulus crossed the  ±35° azimuth line from its original position. If the mouse correctly moved the stimulus 35° to the centre of the screen, it immediately received a 3-μl reward; if it incorrectly moved the stimulus 35° away from the centre, it received a time out. If the mouse responded incorrectly or failed to reach either threshold within the 60-s window, a white-noise burst was played for 500 ms and the inter-trial interval was between 1 and 1.5 s. In trials for which the visual stimulus contrast was set to 0%, the mouse had to respond as for any other trial by turning the wheel in the correct direction (assigned according to the statistics of the prevailing block) to receive a reward, but the mouse was not able to perceive whether the stimulus was presented on the left or right side of the screen. The mouse also received feedback (noise burst or reward) on 0% contrast trials.\\n30\\t\\n31\\tEach session started with 90 trials in which the probability of a visual stimulus appearing on the left or right side was equal. Specifically, the 100%, 25%, 12.5% and 6% contrast trials were each presented 10 times on each side, and the 0% contrast was presented 10 times in total (that is, the ratio of the 100, 25, 12.5, 6 and 0% contrasts were set at 2, 2, 2, 2 and 1, respectively). The side (and thus correct movement) for the 0% contrast trials was chosen randomly between the right and left with equal probability. This initial block of 90 trials is referred to as the unbiased block (50:50).\\n32\\t\\n33\\tAfter the unbiased block, trials were presented in biased blocks: in right-bias blocks, stimuli appeared on the right on 80% of the trials, whereas in left-bias blocks, stimuli appeared on the right on 20% of the trials. The ratio of the contrasts remained as above (2:2:2:2:1). Whether the first biased block in a session was left or right was randomly chosen, and blocks were then alternated. The length of a block was drawn from an exponential distribution with scale parameter of 60 trials, but truncated to lie between 20 and 100 trials.\\n34\\t\\n35\\tThe automated shaping protocol for training involved two collections of sessions. In the first session, the animals started performing a version of the task without biased blocks and were then progressively introduced to harder stimuli with weaker contrasts as they became progressively more competent. They also experienced a debiasing protocol, which was intended to dissuade them from persisting with just one of the choices. Once they were performing sufficiently well on all non-zero contrasts, they were faced with the biased blocks. When, in turn, performance on those was adequate (including on 0% contrast trials, which are informed by the block), they graduated to recording. The neural regressors were defined by binning the spike counts from each neuron in each session in a given region in a specific time window on each trial. The duration of the time window, the number of bins in that time window (that is, the bin size) and the trial event to which it was aligned depended on the variable that is the target of our regression (Supplementary Table 2). everything is loaded through `ONE` / `brainbox` loaders, never by reading files directly.\\n\\nKey variables:\\n- `trials` table (20 columns): `stimOn_times`, `goCue_times`, `goCueTrigger_times`,\\n  `firstMovement_times`, `response_times`, `feedback_times`, `feedbackType`, `choice`,\\n  `contrastLeft`, `contrastRight`, `probabilityLeft`, `rewardVolume`, `intervals_0/1`,\\n  `stimOff_times`, `quiescencePeriod`, …\\n  - `choice ∈ {-1, 0, +1}`; verified empirically (see Step 4) that `choice == +1` is a **left**\\n    report and `choice == -1` a **right** report; `0` = no-go.\\n  - `probabilityLeft ∈ {0.2, 0.5, 0.8}`.\\n- `wheel`: `SessionLoader.load_wheel()` returns position interpolated to 1 kHz plus Gaussian-smoothed\\n  `velocity`/`acceleration`.\\n- `leftCamera.ROIMotionEnergy` (whisker motion energy) at ~60 Hz; `rightCamera` at ~150 Hz.\\n- clusters table after `merge_clusters`: IBL QC metrics (`amp_median`, `noise_cutoff`,\\n  `slidingRP_viol`, `label`, `firing_rate`, …) plus Allen `acronym` per cluster.\\n\\n### Dataset Size (from data files / release table)\\n| Statistic | Value |\\n|-----------|-------|\\n| Sessions (BWM freeze `bwm_release.csv`) | 459 |\\n| Probe insertions | 699 (701 probe dirs staged) |\\n| Subjects | 139 |\\n| Sessions / subject | 1–?
